field.label: Enable
field.help: Record which LAN hosts used which ports and services, based on the firewall state table.

field.label: LAN interfaces
field.help: The subnets (including virtual IPs) of these interfaces are treated as your LAN / customer hosts. Their devices are also used for passive ARP listening (bridges are replaced by their members). In transparent bridge mode the interfaces usually have no IP address: add the customer subnets below.

field.label: Additional networks
field.help: Extra customer networks in CIDR notation, e.g. routed or bridged VDS public subnets (203.0.113.0/24).

field.label: Ignore firewall traffic
field.help: Do not record the firewall's own addresses as hosts, and skip connections the firewall itself started (including service tests).

field.label: Answered connections only
field.help: Only count connections the other side answered. Keeps port scans and unanswered attempts out of the statistics.

field.label: Record remote addresses
field.help: Keep per remote address detail (who talked to whom). Disable on very busy hosts to keep the database small.

field.label: Poll interval (seconds)
field.help: How often the state table is read. Connections shorter than this may be missed.

field.label: Automatic service test
field.help: When a LAN host is seen serving a port, connect to it from the firewall and identify the service (banner, HTTP, TLS, Redis, PostgreSQL, RDP, DNS, NTP...).

field.label: Tests per minute
field.help: Maximum number of ports tested per cycle (one cycle per minute).

field.label: Never test ports
field.help: Comma separated ports or ranges that are never connected to, e.g. 25,8000-8100. They are still listed by port name.

field.label: Use nmap
field.help: Use nmap -sV (version-light) first when /usr/local/bin/nmap is installed (pkg install nmap). Slower but recognises more services.

field.label: Alert on LAN to LAN traffic
field.help: Connections between two LAN hosts (e.g. one customer VDS to another) can indicate lateral movement. All of them are recorded and listed under LAN to LAN; this selects which ones also raise an alert (one per source, destination and port per day). Scans always alert unless this is off.

field.label: Trusted networks
field.help: Addresses or networks, inside or outside (e.g. backup, monitoring or management servers). Block conditions and automatic filtering never block them, and their LAN to LAN connections and scans never raise an alert (they are still recorded).

field.label: Also read the firewall log
field.help: Only useful when block rules log. Without logging, blocked traffic is seen through sampling and rule counters (see Blocked traffic below).

field.label: Scan threshold: hosts
field.help: Alert when one LAN host contacts at least this many other LAN hosts within 5 minutes.

field.label: Scan threshold: ports
field.help: Alert when one LAN host tries at least this many different LAN host/port combinations within 5 minutes.

field.label: Sample blocked traffic
field.help: Every poll, listen for a short, bounded time to connection attempts only (TCP SYN, UDP, ICMP echo) and check them against the pf state table: an attempt without a state was blocked. Cost stays fixed during an attack (time and packet cap), nothing is logged to disk. Numbers are estimates.

field.label: Sample interfaces
field.help: Leave empty for automatic: the LAN interfaces and, for a transparent bridge, every member of the bridge (attacks from outside arrive on the upstream member). On a routed firewall add the WAN interface to also see blocked inbound attacks.

field.label: Sample time (seconds)
field.help: Listening time per poll and interface. The poll takes this much longer.

field.label: Sample packet cap
field.help: Stop listening earlier once this many attempts were captured; protects the firewall during floods. The rate is scaled up accordingly.

field.label: Blocked outbound alert (pkt/s)
field.help: Alert when a LAN host sends at least this many blocked packets per second (spam, scanning, compromised host).

field.label: Blocked inbound alert (pkt/s)
field.help: Alert when at least this many packets per second towards one LAN host are blocked (attack in progress; critical at 10x).

field.label: Block rule alert (pkt/s)
field.help: Alert when one block rule drops at least this many packets per second. Exact, from the pf rule counters.

field.label: Track MAC / IP bindings
field.help: Read the ARP / NDP tables and alert when a MAC uses more than one IPv4 address, when a MAC changes its IP, or when an IP moves to another MAC (IP taken over, ARP spoofing, IP conflict).

field.label: Change window (hours)
field.help: A MAC using another IP within this period counts as an IP change (or as multiple IPs when both are active).

field.label: Ignore MAC addresses
field.help: Comma separated MACs that legitimately use many addresses, e.g. the upstream gateway (one IP per customer subnet) or a router doing proxy ARP. VRRP/CARP virtual MACs are always ignored.

field.label: MAC / IP source
field.help: A transparent bridge has (almost) no ARP entries of its own, so MAC / IP bindings are learned by passively listening to ARP and IPv6 neighbour discovery (tcpdump) on the selected interfaces.

field.label: Warning threshold: states per LAN host
field.help: Alert when one LAN host holds at least this many firewall states (critical at twice the value). Typical for a DDoS target or a host flooding / scanning out. This is only an alert threshold of HostGuard, it does not limit anything: pf limits per rule (max, max-src-*) and the state table in total, those are read from the rules automatically.

field.label: Warning threshold: new connections per second
field.help: Alert when one LAN host opens (or receives) at least this many new connections per second. Alert threshold only, not a pf limit (a rule's max-src-conn-rate is).

field.label: State table warning (%)
field.help: Alert when the pf state table is this full (critical at 95%). Increases of pf limit counters (memory, state-limit, src-limit, max-src-conn(-rate), overload, synflood, NAT map failures) and rules close to their "max states" always alert.

field.label: Shaper drop alert (pkt/s)
field.help: Alert when the traffic shaper drops at least this many packets per second for one address (per IP pipe / queue) or for a shared pipe, i.e. the bandwidth limit is reached. Limits, masks and descriptions are read from Firewall: Shaper.

field.label: Attack threshold (pkt/s)
field.help: Open an attack episode when one LAN host receives at least this many connection attempts / UDP packets per second from outside (estimated from sampling, blocked and passed). Each episode is classified: SYN flood, UDP flood, ICMP flood, reflection / amplification (UDP from DNS, NTP, memcached, SSDP, CLDAP ... source ports), distributed brute force, port scan.

field.label: Use Suricata alerts
field.help: Read Suricata alerts (eve.json, Services: Intrusion Detection) whose destination is a LAN host and show them per host and per source. Suricata must write its EVE log to /var/log/suricata/eve.json.

field.label: Use CrowdSec decisions
field.help: Read the local CrowdSec decisions (cscli decisions list) every few minutes to show why an outside address is banned (scenario, e.g. ssh-bf, http-probing).

field.label: Watch pf tables
field.help: Alert when a LAN host appears in a pf table whose name contains one of these words, e.g. virusprot (connection limit overload), sshlockout, crowdsec.

field.label: Owner and network type of sources
field.help: Once a day (once more three hours after a download that missed a list) download free public lists (no account needed, about 15 MB a day, about 35 MB on disk): iptoasn.com (owner AS and country), the address ranges AWS, Google Cloud, Oracle, DigitalOcean, Linode, Cloudflare, Fastly and the Tor Project publish, the official lists rezmoss/cloud-provider-ip-addresses collects (Azure, CDNs, search engine and AI crawlers, monitoring, iCloud Private Relay ...), X4BNet lists_vpn (hosting and VPN ranges), ipverse/as-metadata (ISP / business / hosting / education / government per AS) and Spamhaus ASN-DROP. Where lists disagree the official ones win; the AS category is only an estimate and used last. Lookups are local; no address is sent anywhere.

field.label: Also hosting
field.help: AS numbers to label as hosting in addition to the lists, e.g. AS16276 (OVH), AS24940 (Hetzner), AS51167 (Contabo).

field.label: Automatic filtering
field.help: Put outside sources into virusprot automatically, graded by how sure the detection is. Level 1 (certain, practically no false positives): a source whose blocked TCP SYNs or UDP packets from a client port (not traceroute / mtr) reach 20 ports of one host or 10 LAN hosts within one sample (a few seconds), blocked traffic from a Spamhaus ASN-DROP network. Level 2 (likely): repeated logins in a distributed brute force (not on mail and web login ports, whose clients open several connections at once), alerts Suricata dropped itself (IPS mode, the rules your policy sets to drop; in IDS mode nothing is dropped and this matches nothing). The Suricata severity is not used: it is the priority of the signature's class (a policy-violation alert such as a curl user agent is severity 1), not how sure the match is. Level 3 (possible, mistakes likelier with shared addresses / CGNAT): repeat sources of floods that pf also blocked, sources over a per source rule limit. Never: LAN hosts, the firewall, trusted networks, search engine / AI crawlers, monitoring probes, iCloud Private Relay, CDNs (these need "Owner and network type of sources"), and reflection sources (abused DNS / NTP servers). The source of SYN / UDP packets can be forged, so someone could get an address blocked on purpose: add your own monitoring and management addresses and outside addresses that must never be blocked (customer offices, payment / webhook senders) to the trusted networks. The rules show up on the Block conditions tab. Disabling HostGuard itself leaves what is blocked at that moment in virusprot: set this to off first.

field.label: Automatic filtering: block for (hours)
field.help: How long an automatically blocked address stays in virusprot after its last match (with an escalating ban: the first time). A changed value also applies to the addresses blocked already.

field.label: Automatic filtering: ban type
field.help: Fixed: every block lasts the time above. Escalating: an address blocked again by the same rule stays twice as long as the time before (24 h, 48 h, 96 h ...) up to the longest block below; once its last block ended 30 days ago it starts at the first step again. Block conditions you add yourself choose their own ban type on the Block conditions tab.

field.label: Automatic filtering: longest block (hours)
field.help: With an escalating ban, the longest a block grows to (720 hours = 30 days). Never shorter than the first block.
